newsitem.title: USA: Moussa says Israel actions threaten peace process.
newsitem.headline: Moussa says Israel actions threaten peace process.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Friday that Israeli actions had "gravely affected" the credibility of the Middle East peace process, creating an atmosphere of pessimism.
In a speech in Washington on the eve of a visit by President Hosni Mubarak, Moussa said Egypt looked to the United States to play an "active role" as honest broker to get the process back on track.

He was speaking in the wake of Israeli decisions to build 6,500 new Jewish homes in East Jerusalem and close down four Palestinian offices there. The moves have infuriated the Palestinians and irritated the United States.
Moussa hit out at what he called "a return to the illegal policy of settlements" and "actions that would alter the status of Jerusalem," and declared: "All those policies will have to stop."

"The absence of good faith on the part of any of the parties would adversely affect the (peace) process and create an atmosphere of pessimism," Moussa told the National Association of Arab Americans in a luncheon speech.

"I am sorry to say that this atmosphere is there, is prevailing, and that the credibility of the peace process itself has been gravely affected by the actions I have referred to. Nobody can have their cake and eat it."
The Egyptian minister later discussed the Israeli action at a meeting with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

He told reporters afterwards that U.S. displeasure had been conveyed to Israel. "I of course add to that, this is the position of the (United) States, but our position is that it is also illegal and it is also detrimental to the peace process," he said.

In his luncheon speech, Moussa declined comment on an overnight decision by the Israeli cabinet to withdraw troops from a small part of the West Bank, saying Egypt first wanted to consult Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. PLO officials have denounced the pullout as insufficient.

Mubarak, who arrives on Saturday, is the latest in a procession of Middle East leaders to come to Washington. Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have both visited recently and King Hussein of Jordan is due this month.
Moussa made clear that Egypt would be pressing Washington to take a firm line with Israel.

"We are looking forward for an active role to be played by the United States and we are ready to do the same," he said. "The role of the United States as an honest broker should be promoted, should be preserved, because the role of the U.S. ... is very much a must."
Moussa said it was unthinkable that the Middle East should still be talking about Palestinian problems and Israeli expansion policies into the year 2000.

"We'll have to finish that," he said. "By the end of this decade ... a peace agreement will have to be achieved, Israeli forces will have to withdraw from the territories occupied in 1967, the Palestinian rights should be fully met and relations of peace would be established," he said.
